TaxoTox Reference Validation — Diagnostic Report

Generated: 2026-04-05 07:06 | ECOTOX rows: 118146 | Reference rows: 12254 | Reference source: taxotox_reference.fst | CompTox gap-fill: YES (3889 predictions) | Mode of Action: YES (12254 / 12254 rows assigned) | Benchmarks: YES

This report validates the taxotox_reference.fst table produced by taxotox_install.R . It covers four areas: (1) correctness of the HC5 computation pipeline (Species Sensitivity Distribution fitting and empirical scaling); (2) the assumption that LC50 and EC50 are interchangeable for Toxic Unit calculations; (3) the quality of CompTox/OPERA gap-fill predictions relative to measured ECOTOX data; and (4) coverage of the Mode of Action classification used by the CAMA method. All plots are interactive — hover for compound details, click legend entries to isolate groups.

1. HC5 Coverage Summary

What this shows: a single summary of coverage across all install steps. n_ecotox_data = rows with a measured ECOTOX median (the primary TU denominator). SSD / Both / Scaled = HC5 method coverage: SSD = full log-normal Species Sensitivity Distribution fitted from ECOTOX data (n ≥ 5); Both = SSD + scaling factor computed; Scaled = scaling factor only. n_predicted = CompTox/OPERA predictions available (fish and crustacean only; algae has no suitable endpoint). n_moa_assigned = rows with a Mode of Action group assigned. n_moa_specific = rows assigned to a specific mechanism (acetylcholinesterase inhibition, Photosystem II inhibition, pyrethroid, or reactive) rather than the default narcosis. Columns not shown are absent because that install step has not been run yet.

2. HC5 (SSD-fitted) vs Median LC50 [log–log]

What this shows: the relationship between the SSD-derived HC5 and the median LC50 for all data-rich compound×group pairs (n ≥ 5). Expected pattern: a tight log-linear cloud with slope ≈ 1, offset below the 1:1 line by log₁₀(k). The solid coloured lines show the theoretical position y = x × k for each group; the dotted lines are OLS fits to the actual data. What to look for: OLS slope close to 1 (proportional scaling), OLS intercept close to the k-line (scaling factor is unbiased), low scatter around the fit (k is a good predictor). Point size is proportional to n_ecotox.

3. Scaled HC5 vs SSD-fitted HC5 (agreement)

What this shows: direct comparison between the two HC5 estimates for all data-rich rows. x-axis = hc5_model_ng_L (median × k); y-axis = hc5_ssd_ng_L (full SSD). Expected pattern: points along the 1:1 diagonal. What to look for: systematic offset above or below the diagonal indicates that k over- or under-estimates HC5 at the extremes of the LC50 range (heteroscedasticity). Wide scatter quantifies the uncertainty in using the scaling factor for data-poor compounds. This plot is empty if taxotox_reference.fst was not yet updated with the scaling factor (re-run install).

4. Median LC50 vs Median EC50 (endpoint interchangeability)

What this shows: for compounds where both LC50 and EC50 data exist in ECOTOX, this plots their separate medians against each other. Why it matters: TaxoTox combines LC50 and EC50 into a single median before computing TU. This is standard practice (Backhaus & Faust, 2012) but rests on the assumption that the two endpoint types produce similar concentration estimates for acute aquatic toxicity. Expected pattern: points near the 1:1 line. What to look for: systematic divergence (e.g. EC50 consistently lower than LC50 for a group) would indicate the endpoints should be kept separate in the aggregation step.

5. Distribution of k = HC5 (SSD) / Median LC50

What this shows: the distribution of the HC5/median ratio across all data-rich compounds, separately per taxonomic group. The dashed vertical line marks the group median (the k value used in the scaling factor). Why it matters: k is assumed constant within each group. If the distribution is narrow and unimodal, this assumption holds well. What to look for: a narrow peak centred on the median line = low uncertainty in scaled HC5 estimates; a wide or bimodal distribution = k is a poor predictor for some compound classes and scaled HC5 estimates carry substantial uncertainty.

7. Denominator Coverage by Source

What this shows: how many compound×group rows have a usable TU denominator, broken down by data source. Blue = ECOTOX median only (most reliable). Green = compound present in both ECOTOX and CompTox (can be cross-validated). Orange = CompTox prediction only, no ECOTOX data (gap-fill rows, n_ecotox = 0). Grey = no denominator available (algae gap-fill not possible; some CAS not in CompTox). Why it matters: orange rows represent the net gain from the I-2 gap-fill step; compounds in grey will still produce no TU contribution in the app.

8. Mode of Action Group Coverage

What this shows: how many compound×group rows in the reference table have been assigned to a Mode of Action group, and how each was classified. Blue = classified by chemical name pattern matching (highest confidence — captures major pesticide classes: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, Photosystem II inhibitors, pyrethroids, reactive chemicals). Orange = classified by LogKow (Verhaar scheme) where no name pattern matched. Grey = default assignment to narcosis (no name pattern or LogKow available). Why it matters: for the Concentration Addition with Mode of Action grouping (CAMA) method to produce results that differ from standard Concentration Addition, compounds in the same sample must span multiple Mode of Action groups. A table dominated by 'narcosis' means CAMA will return the same result as standard TU/PTI for most samples.


10. SSD vs Scaled HC5 — Largest Discrepancies

What this shows: the full table of compound×group rows where both HC5 methods were computed, sorted by |log2(SSD/Scaled)| — largest disagreements first. Use this table to identify specific compounds where the scaling factor performs poorly and where caution is warranted when interpreting HC5-based TU outputs.
